title: Why the Octet Rule Breaks Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
A pairs game leaves one child alone, a cricket team plays with ten, and a big lift carries twelve, not eight. Rules that work most days can break. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 4, Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure) we find exactly where the octet rule breaks, and why.

On the molecule bench, three chlorine atoms share electrons with boron and an octet meter stops at six: an incomplete octet (LiCl, BeH2, BCl3). Eleven electrons of NO drop into pairs and one is left alone: an odd electron molecule (NO, NO2). Phosphorus and sulphur fill the meter to ten and twelve in PF5 and SF6: the expanded octet, possible because period 3 atoms have 3d orbitals. A worked example sorts BeCl2, PCl5 and SCl2, then we cover the other drawbacks (XeF2, KrF2, XeOF2, no shapes, no energy), the PCl5 versus NCl5 exam trap, an original exam pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 42 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students. For NCERT, CBSE, ICSE/ISC, PUC, NEET and JEE students.
